snippet.title: The Walking Ape - Why We Still Move Like Hunters | Why Walking Heals Us
snippet.description:
A deep-time documentary exploring the oldest human instinct: movement.
Why do we walk to think? Why does a quiet path calm the nervous system?
And why does our entire body feel designed for distances we almost never use?
  In this Sleepless Homo episode, we follow the story of walking from the earliest hominins millions of years ago to the modern mind.
From bipedal origins and long-range tracking, to endurance physiology, climate migrations, sensory intelligence, emotional regulation, and the quiet ancestral memory that still lives in your body - this is the full evolutionary story of why humans walk, and why walking still heals us today.
If you’ve ever wondered why a simple walk clears your thoughts, softens your anxiety, or reconnects you to something older than language, this episode is for you.

🕯️ The story of humanity… told softly.

snippet.title: 13. The Assyrians - Empire of Iron
snippet.description:
In the lowlands of Northern Iraq, a series of enormous cities lie crumbling in ruins...

In this episode, find out about one of the most remarkable ancient civilizations: the society known today as the neo-Assyrian Empire. Discover how the Assyrians built their empire out of the ashes of the Bronze Age, and built an empire of iron that lasted for centuries. Explore the extraordinary flourishing of art and technology that they fostered. And finally, discover what happened to cause their final, devastating collapse.

snippet.title: The Last Letters from Ugarit | What Happens When Help Never Comes?
snippet.description:
The last days of Ugarit were not a mystery written in myth. They were written in logistics. In clay tablets. In sealed orders. In urgent messages that still assumed the network would reply. This episode follows the real archaeological record from Ras Shamra on the Syrian coast, where Late Bronze Age scribes kept writing as the wider Eastern Mediterranean system began to fail. You will hear how a port city lives by schedules, how archives function like a nervous system, why delays become deadly, and what it means when “help” is real on paper but impossible in practice. We trace Ugarit’s world through tablets, harbor infrastructure, diplomatic correspondence, and burn layers that accidentally preserved the city’s last paperwork by firing it into permanence. We look at how trust-based networks fracture under stress, how triage quietly decides which places receive resources, and why collapse is often experienced not as one loud event, but as unanswered messages and empty horizons.
  If you use these videos to sleep, study, drive, or think at night, tell me how you listen.

snippet.title: How The French KILLED Louis XVI And the MANUAL They Followed
snippet.description:
A History for Sleep documentary. 

On the morning of 21 January 1793, the French Revolution executed Louis XVI — and every detail of his death had been engineered around a book the French had been studying for months.
The English had killed their king in 1649 and watched him become a martyr. The French had read that story. They had read it carefully. By the autumn of 1792, accounts of Charles I's execution were a bestseller in Paris bookshops, on the desks of the deputies preparing the trial, and even in the prison cell of Louis XVI himself, who was using the same book to plan his own defense.

This is the story of how that morning was designed. Hour by hour, from the king waking in the Temple at 5 a.m., to the carriage moving through 80,000 troops in heavy fog, to the executioner — a man whose family had served the kings of France for four generations — waiting at the scaffold with four pistols hidden under his coat. To the drum roll that drowned out the king's last words at 10:22 a.m. To the quicklime grave that erased his body by nightfall. To the baby born nine miles from the empty square in the first hours of a country that no longer had a king.
The English had killed a king and lost him to a book. The French had killed a king and made sure no book would come.
This is the story of how they did it — and what the world looked like the morning after.

⏱ CHAPTERS
0:00 — The Hook: Robespierre's Promise
05:54 — The Manual: How the English Failed in 1649
16:58 — The Man in the Cell: Louis XVI's Final Hours
30:13 — The Terrified City: 80,000 Troops in the Fog
42:43 — The Executioner: A Royalist at the Scaffold
51:06 — The Drum Roll: The Reversal Point
50:38 — The Aftermath: Quicklime, an Empty Square, a Manufactured Saint
1:02:10 — Did It Work? The Two-Century Verdict
01:14:11 — The Echo: The First Night Without a King

📖 PRIMARY SOURCES
1. Edgeworth de Firmont, Henry Essex. Mémoires. Published 1815. 
2. The confessor's own account of Louis XVI's last hours.
3. Cléry, Jean-Baptiste. Journal de ce qui s'est passé à la tour du Temple. 
4. Louis XVI's valet, who served him through every day of his imprisonment.
5. Sanson family papers and Memoirs of the Sansons (compiled by Henri-Clément Sanson, descendant of the executioner). Source for the executioner's documented anxiety and the threatening note delivered the night before the execution.
6. Archives parlementaires. Session transcripts of the National Convention, including Robespierre's 3 December 1792 speech naming Charles I and Mary Queen of Scots.
7. Walzer, Michael, ed. Regicide and Revolution: Speeches at the Trial of Louis XVI. Cambridge University Press. For the trial debates and the citation of English precedent.
8. Damoureau, vicar of la Madeleine. Eyewitness account of the burial of Louis XVI in the cemetery of la Madeleine, 21 January 1793.

Where the historical record is contested — most notably the question of who ordered the drum roll that silenced Louis's last words — this documentary acknowledges the ambiguity rather than resolving it falsely.

A long-form historical documentary for sleep, focus, and deep listening. 73 minutes. Calm narration throughout.
Subjects covered: the French Revolution, the execution of Louis XVI, Charles I of England (1649), the trial of Louis XVI, the National Convention, Maximilien Robespierre, Antoine Santerre, Charles-Henri Sanson, Abbé Edgeworth de Firmont, the Temple prison, the Place de la Révolution, the guillotine, the Eikon Basilike, the Bourbon Restoration, the Paris Commune, and the long arc of European regicide from 1649 to 1918.

snippet.title: Kate Crawford | Mapping Empires
snippet.description:
Just as linear perspective restructured how people recognized reality, generative AI is generating a new visual and political language. 

During the talk, Crawford gave us a tour through her detailed artwork Calculating Empires. Through examples ranging from Liebig’s critique of agriculture “robbing” soil nutrients to Faraday’s latex-based electrical insulation that devastated rubber forests, Crawford showed how technologies have long created “metabolic rifts”: systems that extract more than they regenerate.
AI, she suggested, is the newest metabolic rift. Its ingestion cycle—massive-scale data collection prized for quantity over quality—acts like poor nutrition at planetary scale. 

In the closing Q&A, Kevin Kelly asked what responsible, non-extractive AI might look like. Crawford imagined systems built on regenerative energy, consent-based data, and the ability to analyze their own biases and disparities. These futures aren’t impossible, just contested. Our task, Crawford urged, is to create new maps for an AI-shaped era and chart paths that protect the public interest and autonomy.

This talk was presented November 12, 02025 at the Cowell Theater in San Francisco.

snippet.description:

The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse explained through 2,000 years of history, art, and political survival. 
Discover how John of Patmos, Albrecht Dürer, and the Roman Empire shaped the most terrifying image in the Book of Revelation.

The Book of Revelation names exactly one horseman. The other three riders were given their modern identities by a combination of medieval panics, Renaissance engravings, and 20th-century pop culture. The original text was never meant to be a literal schedule of future disasters. 

As apocalyptic literature, Revelation was coded political resistance written by a prisoner targeting the Roman Empire. snippet.title: The Fall of Constantinople: Why No One Came to Save It
snippet.description:
The fall of Constantinople in 1453 is one of the most consequential events in the history of the world. But almost everything you have heard about it is wrong.
The conquest of Constantinople is remembered as an Ottoman triumph. A story of superior firepower, brilliant strategy, and unstoppable force. What that story leaves out is the five decades before the first cannon fired. Because Constantinople did not fall because its enemies were too strong. It fell because the Pope, Venice, Genoa, Hungary, and the entire Christian world looked at what was coming and chose to do nothing.
This is the full story of the fall of the Eastern Roman Empire. From the founding of the city by Constantine the Great to the last night inside the Hagia Sophia. From the thousand years of sieges the walls survived to the fifty-three days that ended everything. From the betrayal of the Fourth Crusade in 1204 to the silence that followed May 29, 1453.
The fall of Constantinople did not just end a city. It ended the Roman Empire. It scattered the scholars who ignited the Renaissance. It closed the trade routes that sent Portugal and Spain into the Atlantic and produced the Age of Exploration. It changed the world in ways that have never fully been acknowledged.
This is the history of Constantinople from the beginning to the end. The city that held for a thousand years. And the civilisation that let it fall.

snippet.title: The American Civil War: The Men Who Made It Inevitable
snippet.description:
The American Civil War killed over 700,000 Americans. History blames Jefferson Davis and Robert E. Lee. But the men who actually built the conditions for that war were George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, and Henry Clay. This is their account.
This full-length American Civil War documentary goes beyond the battles and generals to examine the founding decisions, the broken compromises, and the named individuals whose choices made the bloodiest war in American history unavoidable. From the Constitutional Convention of 1787 to the fall of Reconstruction in 1877, this is the real history of the American Civil War.
What you will learn in this documentary: why the Founding Fathers built slavery into the Constitution, how Thomas Jefferson owned 607 enslaved people while writing that all men are created equal, why George Washington secretly rotated enslaved people out of Pennsylvania to avoid their freedom, how Henry Clay's compromises expanded slavery rather than containing it, why the Kansas-Nebraska Act destroyed the last political boundary between slave and free territory, what Abraham Lincoln actually said about slavery before the Emancipation Proclamation, and why Reconstruction's failure made the Civil War's sacrifices only half count.
This American Civil War history covers: the causes of the Civil War, the role of slavery in the Civil War, the Constitutional Convention and the three-fifths compromise, the Missouri Compromise, the Compromise of 1850 and the Fugitive Slave Act, the Kansas-Nebraska Act and Bleeding Kansas, the Dred Scott decision, John Brown and Harpers Ferry, the 1860 presidential election and secession, the Emancipation Proclamation, the United States Colored Troops, the Battle of Antietam, the Battle of Gettysburg, the Siege of Vicksburg, Sherman's March to the Sea, Appomattox, and the rise and fall of Reconstruction.
If you are looking for a Civil War documentary that takes history seriously, names names, and does not look away from what the evidence actually shows, this is it.

snippet.title: Hitler’s Cultural Purge: Art and Media Under Nazi Rule | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
He was a failed artist who couldn't paint people. Rejected twice by the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts, Adolf Hitler never forgot the humiliation. When he came to power, his revenge wasn't just political. It was cultural. Within years, every artist, writer, musician, filmmaker, and architect in Germany had to register with the state, prove their racial identity, and conform to a single, centrally controlled vision of what art was allowed to be. Those who refused lost their licence to work. Those who couldn't comply fled. The rest were watched. What followed was one of the most sophisticated and terrifying propaganda systems ever constructed, built not on screaming speeches alone, but on cinema, radio, architecture, and the deliberate manipulation of taste. And at the centre of it all was a question that nobody in the regime could agree on: what does Nazi art actually look like?

snippet.title: The Complete History of SWITZERLAND: From Alps to Modern Power
snippet.description:
Journey through the complete history of Switzerland in one immersive documentary. From Celtic Helvetii and Roman frontier towns to medieval trade routes and the birth of the Swiss Confederacy, we trace how geography, law, and cooperation forged a unique state. Watch decisive moments unfold: victories over Burgundy, the Reformation’s civic experiments in Zurich and Geneva, Westphalian recognition of independence, and the Sonderbund War that led to the federal constitution of eighteen forty-eight. See how tunnels, railways, and direct democracy powered industry and connected valleys, and how neutrality was tested in both world wars. We examine prosperity and participation in the twentieth century, women’s suffrage, Jura’s creation, environmental reform, and the rise of precision industry, life sciences, and finance. Finally, we explore Switzerland in a globalized Europe—bilateral accords, humanitarian leadership from Geneva, energy transition, digital innovation, and modern challenges.
If you’re curious how a small, multilingual country balanced sovereignty with interdependence—and turned alpine passes into arteries of trade and ideas—this is your guide. Clear storytelling, rigorous research, and human moments make complex history accessible. Subscribe for more deep, documentary-style histories.

snippet.title: From Caltrops To Mines: The Evolution Of Ambush Weapons | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Ambush warfare has been a decisive tactic for centuries, allowing smaller or weaker forces to defeat stronger opponents through surprise and positioning. From ancient battlefields to modern conflicts, weapons designed to remain hidden until the last moment have transformed the way wars are fought. Early tools like caltrops, used as far back as antiquity, could stop cavalry charges and control entire battlefields by making terrain impassable.

With the development of firearms in the 18th and 19th centuries, soldiers gained the ability to fire rifles from a prone position, increasing accuracy while staying concealed. In the 20th century, the introduction of land mines added a new level of danger, creating invisible threats that could strike at any time. This story explores how ambush tactics evolved over time, combining technology and strategy to create some of the most effective and feared methods of warfare.

snippet.title: Life in the Mesolithic Age | The Forgotten Stone Age
snippet.description:
Tonight, drift back to the Mesolithic age, the forgotten chapter of the Stone Age, and discover what life was actually like in the most overlooked age in the whole human story. This is history for sleep, told slowly and gently, made to quiet a busy mind and carry you down into deep and restful sleep.

The Mesolithic is the Middle Stone Age, the long bridge between two famous others. Behind it lies the Old Stone Age, the time of the great hunters, of the mammoth and the painted cave. Ahead of it lies the New Stone Age, the time of the first farmers and the first villages. For a very long time, people decided that nothing of importance happened on that bridge at all. They called it a gap, a dull pause, the age that everyone agreed to forget. They were wrong. This forgotten age was one of the great turning points of the whole human story.

For here, in this so-called empty pause, human beings quietly invented almost everything the famous ages would be built upon. This is the age of the bow, drawn and loosed at last across the world. The age of the boat upon the water. The age of the dog, the first animal ever to walk at a human side. And it is the age of the greatest change of all, the age when a wandering people first looked at a stretch of river and thought, not we will pass through here, but we will stay. That quiet moment of settling down was the hinge on which everything after would turn.

Across one slow turning of the year, you will live inside this world. You will wake by the water in the green heart of the age. You will learn the bow and glide out in a dugout canoe through the morning mist. You will gather along the rivers and the giving shores, meet the scattered peoples of the forest and the coast, and come to understand why this forgotten age matters more than the famous ones on either side of it.

There is no need to stay awake for any of it. If sleep comes early and carries you off before the boat ever leaves the bank, that is exactly as it should be. The river is patient. It has been flowing a very long time, and the story will still be here. Let the calm voice, the still water, and the green quiet be the last things you remember tonight.

If these long, quiet journeys into the deep past help you find rest, following along is the simplest way to let more of them reach you, on other nights when the dark feels wide and sleep is slow to come.

Rest well, and let the forgotten age carry you gently into sleep.

snippet.title: How the Vikings Became Kings of Europe: The Full History
snippet.description:
They came as raiders. They left as kings.
Within two centuries of the first Norse longship beaching on an English shore, men of Scandinavian blood sat on the throne of England, governed the north of France, founded the cities that became Russia, carved out a kingdom in Sicily, and stood guard inside the imperial palace in Constantinople. This is the viking history documentary that tells the story most treatments never reach: not the raids, but what came after.
The history of the vikings is not a story of destruction. It is a story of the most consequential political transformation in medieval Europe, driven by landless men with the best ships in the world and an instinct for power that no kingdom on the continent could stop.
This is the full history. From Lindisfarne to the Norman Conquest. From the Danelaw to the Varangian Guard. From a longship on the North Sea to the thrones of England, France, Sicily, and Byzantium.

snippet.title: The ENTIRE Story of Ancient Mythology – Full Detailed Documentary
snippet.description:
Explore the full journey of Roman mythology in this comprehensive documentary, tracing its evolution from ancient Italian spirit beliefs to the complex pantheon that shaped one of history’s greatest empires. This film uncovers how early agricultural traditions, Etruscan influences, and Greek storytelling blended to form Rome’s unique religious identity. Follow the legendary path of Aeneas, the foundation of Rome by Romulus, and the creation of early priesthoods under Numa.

As Rome expands, discover how public rituals, temples, household worship, and the rise of foreign cults helped define Roman daily life. Learn how political leaders used religion to gain power, how the imperial cult placed emperors at the center of sacred life, and how provincial cultures transformed Roman beliefs across Europe, Africa, and the Near East.

This documentary also examines the spread of mystery religions, philosophical interpretations of the gods, and the rise of universal deities like Sol Invictus. Finally, witness the dramatic transition from pagan Rome to Christian Rome under Constantine and Theodosius, and how Roman mythology survived as cultural heritage long after its temples closed.
A complete, clear, and deeply researched dive into Rome’s sacred world.

Operation Paperclip was the secret U.S. government program that brought Nazi scientists to America after World War II.

Wernher von Braun, Arthur Rudolph, and 1,600 other German engineers helped build NASA, the Saturn V rocket, and the Apollo program.

On May 2, 1945, with Germany collapsing around him, rocket scientist Wernher von Braun made a calculated decision. He would surrender to Americans, not Soviets, and trade his expertise for a new life in the United States. What followed was one of the largest secret recruitment operations in American history.

Operation Paperclip brought over 1,600 German scientists, engineers, and technicians to the U.S. between 1945 and 1959. Many had been Nazi Party members. Some had used concentration camp labor. Their files were sanitized, their records altered, and their pasts erased. In exchange, they gave America the technological edge it needed to win the Cold War and reach the Moon.

This documentary traces the full arc of Operation Paperclip, from the V-2 rockets that terrorized London to the Saturn V that carried astronauts to the lunar surface. It examines what was gained, what was lost, and the question that remains: what are you willing to sacrifice for victory?

snippet.title: The Opium Wars Were Never About Opium
snippet.description:
Everyone knows the Opium Wars were about opium. A drug, sold by Britain, resisted by China, and a war that followed. But that is not what really happened. Beneath the famous story of the drug lies a deeper one, almost forgotten, about a single metal that the largest empire on Earth could not live without, and could not make for itself. That metal was silver. And it is the true cause of everything that followed.
For three hundred years, China ran on silver. She taxed her people in it, priced everything in it, and built the wealth of the richest empire the world had ever seen upon it, yet her own mines produced almost none. The silver came from the other side of the planet, from a single mountain in the Andes, carried across the widest ocean on Earth into the holds of Chinese ships. So long as it flowed, China grew richer and more certain of her place at the centre of all things. The dependency was invisible, because it paid.
This is the story of what happened when it stopped. Of how Britain, unable to pay for Chinese tea by any honest means, reversed the flow of silver with the one thing that would sell itself, a drug grown in India and smuggled to the Chinese coast. Of the richest man in the world, a Canton merchant whose fortune helped build America and then vanished within a generation. Of the respectable gentlemen who ran the largest drug operation in history and felt no shame in it. And of the incorruptible official who tried to stop them, and lit the fuse of a war that would humble an empire and is remembered in China to this day.
From a mountain of silver to a river of opium, this is the full story of how China's greatest strength became the weakness that brought her down. Settle in, and let the long story carry you off into the quiet of the night.

In 2010, a NASA-backed study boldly announced that we’d found alien life right here on Earth. So where are all these aliens? In this episode of Crash Course Scientific Thinking, we search for the truth and learn how science is an ongoing quest for knowledge that double-checks itself through peer review.
